questions.question_text: Define Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). Explain its basic idea with a suitable example.

answer_key.model_answer:
The Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming approach in which a program is organized around classes and objects rather than only functions and procedures.

An object represents a real-world entity. It contains data (attributes) and functions (methods) that operate on that data.

Example: A Student object may contain data such as name, roll number and marks. Its methods may be study(), displayDetails() and calculateResult().

Thus, OOP organizes a program using objects that combine data and related operations.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 1 mark definition; 2 marks classes/objects idea; 2 marks data and methods; 1 mark suitable example.
answer_key.important_keywords: OOP, classes, objects, real-world entity, attributes, methods, data

questions.question_text: Explain the basic concepts of OOP: class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

answer_key.model_answer:
1. Class: A class is a blueprint or template used to create objects. It defines data members and member functions.
2. Object: An object is an instance of a class. For example, student1 can be an object of the Student class.
3. Encapsulation: It combines data and the functions operating on that data into a single unit, usually a class.
4. Abstraction: It shows essential details and hides unnecessary implementation details. Example: using an ATM without knowing its internal working.
5. Inheritance: It allows one class to acquire properties and methods of another class. Example: Car can inherit from Vehicle.
6. Polymorphism: It means one name or interface can have multiple forms, such as function overloading and method overriding.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 1 mark each for six correctly explained concepts.
answer_key.important_keywords: class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, code reuse

questions.question_text: Differentiate between Procedure-Oriented Programming (POP) and Object-Oriented Programming (OOP).

answer_key.model_answer:
1. POP stands for Procedure-Oriented Programming, while OOP stands for Object-Oriented Programming.
2. POP divides a program into functions or procedures, whereas OOP divides it into classes and objects.
3. POP mainly focuses on functions, whereas OOP mainly focuses on objects and data.
4. In POP, data is generally less protected. OOP protects data using encapsulation and access specifiers.
5. POP follows a top-down approach, whereas OOP generally follows a bottom-up approach.
6. Code reuse is more limited in POP. OOP supports code reuse through inheritance and other mechanisms.
7. Examples of POP are C and Pascal; examples of OOP are C++, Java and C#.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 1 mark for meaning; 4 marks for any four correct differences; 1 mark for examples or approaches.
answer_key.important_keywords: POP, OOP, functions, classes, objects, top-down, bottom-up, encapsulation, inheritance

questions.question_text: Explain the main features of Object-Oriented Programming.

answer_key.model_answer:
1. Class: A blueprint used to create objects; it contains data members and member functions.
2. Object: An instance of a class representing a real-world entity.
3. Encapsulation: Combines data and related functions into one unit and helps protect data.
4. Abstraction: Shows essential information and hides implementation details.
5. Inheritance: Allows a new class to acquire properties and functions of an existing class, promoting code reuse.
6. Polymorphism: Allows one name or interface to have multiple forms, such as function overloading and operator overloading.
7. Data Hiding: Restricts direct access to internal data using private, protected and public access specifiers.
8. Message Passing: Objects communicate by calling methods and passing information.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 1 mark introduction; 5 marks for any five features correctly explained.
answer_key.important_keywords: class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, data hiding, message passing

questions.question_text: Explain the classification of data types in C++ with examples.

answer_key.model_answer:
A data type specifies the kind of data a variable can store. It also determines memory requirements and the operations that can be performed.

1. Basic/Fundamental data types: These are built-in types. Examples: int for integers, char for a character, float and double for decimal values, and bool for true/false values.
2. Derived data types: These are created from fundamental types. Examples: array, pointer, function and reference.
3. User-defined data types: These are created by the programmer. Examples: class, struct, union and enum.
4. Void data type: void represents the absence of a value. It is commonly used for functions that do not return a value, such as void display().
answer_key.marking_rubric: 1 mark definition; 4 marks for the four categories with examples; 1 mark suitable explanation/example of void.
answer_key.important_keywords: basic data types, derived, user-defined, void, int, char, float, array, pointer, class, struct

questions.question_text: What are keywords in C++? Explain their characteristics with suitable examples.

answer_key.model_answer:
Keywords are reserved words in C++ that have a predefined meaning to the compiler. They are part of the language syntax and cannot normally be used as names of variables, functions, classes or other user-defined identifiers.

Examples of C++ keywords include int, float, char, double, if, else, for, while, do, switch, case, break, continue, return, class, public, private, protected, void, const, static, new, delete and this.

Example: int age = 20;
Here, int is a keyword because it specifies the data type. The word age is an identifier because it is the user-defined variable name.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 2 marks definition and characteristics; 2 marks examples; 2 marks explanation of the given statement.
answer_key.important_keywords: reserved words, predefined meaning, compiler, cannot be identifiers, int, class, return, new, delete

questions.question_text: Explain the scope resolution operator (::) and its uses in C++ with examples.

answer_key.model_answer:
The scope resolution operator (::) is used in C++ to identify and access a name within a particular scope.

Uses:
1. Accessing a global variable: If local and global variables have the same name, ::x accesses the global variable.
2. Defining a member function outside a class: Student::display() indicates that display() belongs to the Student class.
3. Accessing static class members: Student::count refers to the static member count of the Student class.
4. Accessing namespace members: std::cout accesses cout from the std namespace.

Thus, :: helps specify the scope to which a name belongs.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 1 mark definition; 4 marks for uses with examples; 1 mark explanation.
answer_key.important_keywords: scope resolution, ::, global variable, class member function, static member, namespace, std::cout

questions.topic: Call by Value and Call by Reference
questions.question_text: Explain call by value and call by reference. Give examples and differentiate between them.

answer_key.model_answer:
1. Call by Value: A copy of the actual value is passed to the function. Changes made to the formal parameter do not affect the original variable.
Example: void change(int x) { x = 50; } If a is 10 and change(a) is called, a remains 10.

2. Call by Reference: A reference or alias to the original variable is passed. Changes made through the reference affect the original variable.
Example: void change(int &x) { x = 50; } If a is 10 and change(a) is called, a becomes 50.

Difference: Call by value passes a copy and does not change the original variable. Call by reference uses a reference parameter with & and can change the original variable.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 2 marks call by value; 2 marks call by reference; 2 marks correct comparison/examples.
answer_key.important_keywords: copy of value, original variable, reference, alias, &, parameter

questions.topic: Difference Between Call by Value, Reference and Pointer
questions.question_text: Differentiate between call by value, call by reference and call by pointer in C++.

answer_key.model_answer:
1. Call by Value: A copy of the variable's value is passed to the function. Changes do not affect the original variable.
2. Call by Reference: A reference (alias) to the original variable is passed. Changes affect the original variable. The parameter is declared using & and the variable is passed directly in the function call.
3. Call by Pointer: The address of the variable is passed to the function. The function uses a pointer parameter and dereferencing (*) to access or modify the original value. The address is commonly passed using &variable.

Main difference: Value passes a copy; reference passes an alias; pointer passes an address that is accessed through a pointer.
answer_key.marking_rubric: 2 marks each for the three methods and their differences.
answer_key.important_keywords: copy, reference, alias, address, pointer, &, *, original variable
